text: Small Dry-Cooled Modular Reactor and Hyperscale Data Center 76 4.1.3 Colorado State Siting a large light-water reactor in the state of Colorado seems ostensibly difficult, which can be seen in Table C1. Looking to the individual exclusion areas, it is easy to see why this is the case. Much of the western half of the state is occupied by the Rocky Mountains, and has associated landslide risks and active faults. Much of the east simply has no access to cooling water from the series of reservoirs in central Colorado. This leaves a narrow, inconsistent band of siting suitability in the middle of Colorado, with some smaller areas Mesa County. Colorado also has several major population centers and airports, which further complicates siting for nuclear projects. In Table C2, the lower cooling water requirement expands viability in eastern Colorado around Pueblo, Fremont, and Custer counties. The higher slope threshold also expands viability in Moffat, Delta, and Rio Blanco. Even still, the counties in the west do not exceed 40% viability. Table C3 shows the siting potential for dry-cooled SMRs, and without cooling water restrictions the vast majority of eastern Colorado is made viable, with most of these counties exceeding 60% suitability. Moffat county also sees a notable boost in suitable land for this same reason. Finally we come to the data center siting in Table C4, which shows that the primary barrier to siting are actually landslide risks in and among the Rocky Mountains, and to a lesser extent the slope of the terrain. Since no other criteria pose significant barriers, most of Colorado has potential for data center development. Table C5 puts into stark relief the significant limitations imposed on water-cooled reactor siting in the state of Colorado, which in turn limits the potential for collocation with data centers. While dry-cooled SMR is usually the more viable technology in western states, this is especially true for Colorado, where the region east of the Rockies dominates the potential for collocation when compared to water-cooled technology. 77 Table C1: Data Package for Large Light Water Reactor for State of Colorado Large LWR (e.g., AP1000) Green –Meets all Criteria Yellow –Single issue Orange –Two issues Blue –3+ issues Composite Map Basemap Percent of Land Available Per County 78 Individual Excluded Area Population (>500 ppsm within 20 miles) SSE (>0.3g) Wetlands/Open Waters Protected Lands Slope (>12% grade) Landslide Risk (High Risk Areas) Floodplain (100-year Risk Areas) Streamflow (<130,000 gpm) Proximity to Hazards Proximity to Fault Lines 79 Table C2: Data Package for Small Modular Reactor for State of Colorado Small Modular Reactor (e.g., AP300) Green –Meets all Criteria Yellow –Single issue Orange –Two issues Blue –3+ issues Composite Map Basemap Percent of Land Available Per County 80 Individual Excluded Area Population (>500 ppsm within 1 miles) SSE (>0.3g) Wetlands/Open Waters Protected Lands Slope (>18% grade) Landslide Risk (High Risk Areas) Floodplain (100-year Risk Areas) Streamflow (<130,000 gpm) Proximity to Hazards Proximity to Fault Lines 81 Table C3: Data Package for Small Dry-Cooled Modular Reactor for State of Colorado Small Dry-Cooled Modular Reactor (e.g., Xe-100) Green –Meets
